result.summary: Pausanias lists the sons of Lycaon and the Arcadian cities they founded or named, including Nyctimus, who inherited the kingdom, and Oenotrus, who sailed to Italy. He then tells of Lycaon's daughter Callisto, whom Zeus loved, Hera turned into a bear, and who became the Great Bear constellation.

scenes.title: Lycaon's sons found Arcadian cities
scenes.summary: Nyctimus inherits the kingdom while his brothers found and name many Arcadian towns. Oenotrus leads the first Greek colony to Italy.

scenes.title: Callisto becomes the Great Bear
scenes.summary: Zeus loves Callisto, Hera turns her into a bear and Artemis shoots her. Hermes saves her child, and she becomes a constellation, though Arcadians show her grave.
scenes.stakes: Callisto is destroyed by Hera's jealousy and Artemis's arrow, and her unborn child is endangered.

analysis.text: The passage ties Arcadian place names to eponymous founders, tracing the land's origins to one royal family.
Pausanias rests on local Arcadian tradition and often cites poets such as Homer and Stesichorus as evidence, while doubting some myths.

legacy.text: Callisto's transformation became a standard explanation for the Great Bear constellation, retold by Ovid and later writers.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias suggests the constellation may simply be named in Callisto's honour, since Arcadians show her tomb.

language_notes.text: "The third generation after Pelasgus" counts descendants of Pelasgus, the legendary first king of Arcadia; Lycaon's sons belong to this generation.
Geryoneis is a lost poem by Stesichorus about Heracles' theft of the cattle of the monster Geryon.
Homer calls Hermes "Acacetes" (often rendered "giver of good"); Pausanias derives it from Acacus, though the true meaning is uncertain.
The Iliad's Catalogue of Ships describes Orchomenus in Arcadia as "rich in flocks"; the bracketed number is the translator's footnote marker.
Odysseus sails from Calypso's island in the Odyssey, steering by the Bear; this is the translation's "Odysseus" for the hero.
"Charles' wain" is an old English name for the Plough or Big Dipper; a wain is a wagon. Bootes is the constellation of the herdsman.

context_notes.text: Lycaon was a legendary early king of Arcadia, a region in the central Peloponnese; Pausanias treats his sons as founders of its towns.
Italy's southern region Oenotria was said to be named for Œnotrus; Greek tradition used this to explain early Greek links with Italy.
Hera, Zeus' wife, was often jealous of his lovers. Artemis, goddess of the hunt, was associated with maidens like Callisto.
Pausanias often mentions graves and local monuments as evidence for or against myths.

literary_notes.text: Cities are named after their founders, a recurring pattern that ties places to legendary heroes.
Many sons set against a single daughter prepares the reader for Callisto's special story.
The story explains the origin of a constellation through Callisto's transformation.
Pausanias's skeptical "perhaps" and appeal to the Arcadians' grave show him weighing rival traditions as a historian.
